stories.title: Two Hours of Sleep Restored in Alzheimer’s Brains in Research Breakthrough
stories.summary: In a groundbreaking study, researchers at the University of Kentucky discovered that microglia—the brain's immune cells—are the main culprits behind sleep loss in Alzheimer's. By temporarily removing these cells in animal models, they restored over two hours of sleep per day. This 'paradigm shifting' finding opens a new target for treating the disease.
stories.extended_summary: Imagine a small fire in your kitchen, but before you can put it out, the sprinklers turn on and soak your entire house. That's what happens in Alzheimer's brains, according to researchers at the University of Kentucky. Amyloid plaques are the fire, and microglia—the brain's immune cells—are the sprinklers, causing widespread damage. The team, led by Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., discovered that these microglia are the primary drivers of sleep loss in Alzheimer's. By using a drug to temporarily remove these cells in animal models, they successfully restored over two hours of sleep per day. This finding, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, is described as 'paradigm shifting' and offers a new target for treating the disease. It's a hopeful step forward in understanding and potentially alleviating one of the most challenging symptoms of Alzheimer's.

stories.title: What makes a park organic?
stories.summary: Durango, Colorado, is proving that parks can be beautiful without synthetic chemicals. Through its Organically Managed Lands Program, the city uses organic fertilizers and biological weed control to keep green spaces healthy. It's a growing movement, with other Colorado towns following suit to create safer, more sustainable parks.
stories.extended_summary: At first glance, Fanto Park in Durango looks like any other city park—green grass, mowed lawns, and shady trees. But a small sign reveals a big difference: it's organically managed. Since 2012, Durango has been transitioning parks to organic practices, using natural fertilizers and biological methods to control weeds instead of synthetic herbicides. The program started with nine parks and now maintains eight, with crews hand-cutting weeds like thistle and relying on insects and fungi to suppress unwanted plants. Durango isn't alone—Boulder has maintained over 60 parks without synthetic pesticides, and Longmont, Golden, and Lakewood are experimenting with similar practices. It's a growing movement that shows you don't need chemicals to keep public spaces vibrant and healthy.

stories.summary: A four-woman street medicine team in Springfield is bringing healthcare directly to the homeless. By meeting people where they are and building trust, they're not just treating medical issues—they're helping people get housed for the first time. It's a patient-driven approach that's changing lives.
stories.extended_summary: For many homeless individuals, seeing a doctor is a rare or even impossible occurrence. But SIU Medicine's new street medicine team in Springfield is changing that. Led by Dr. Kami Harless, the four-woman team hits the streets to meet homeless individuals where they are, offering medical care and building trusting relationships. The approach is patient-driven, with priorities set by the patients themselves, allowing for deeper conversations about substance use, mental health, and chronic diseases. The team's efforts are already paying off—one person who had been on the streets for a long time is about to be housed for the first time ever. 'It was the relationships,' said nurse LaDorise Ramsey. 'They're proud to come tell us, I've got my key.' It's a powerful reminder that healthcare is about more than just medicine—it's about human connection.

stories.title: A boring tile wants to fix the worst problem of ultra-fast mmWave 5G connections for you
stories.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego have come up with a surprisingly simple fix for 5G's millimeter-wave signal problems: cheap reflective tiles that bounce signals around obstacles. No batteries, no electronics—just 3D-printed tiles that redirect signals where they need to go. It could make ultra-fast 5G much more reliable indoors.
stories.extended_summary: Millimeter-wave 5G promises blazing-fast speeds, but it has a major weakness: signals struggle to get around walls, furniture, and even people. Researchers at UC San Diego have developed a surprisingly low-tech solution—passive metasurfaces, essentially 3D-printed reflective tiles that redirect mmWave signals. These tiles don't need batteries, power supplies, or control electronics; they simply bounce signals to where they're needed. This could eliminate the need for expensive additional access points or powered relays, making ultra-fast 5G more practical for indoor use. It's a clever, cost-effective approach that might just solve one of 5G's biggest headaches.

stories.summary: Georgia's marshes are disappearing due to rising tides, but a new plan offers hope: give them space to migrate. Instead of building walls, communities are using 'living shorelines' that mimic nature to combat erosion. It's a forward-thinking approach to preserving these vital ecosystems.
stories.extended_summary: In coastal Liberty County, Georgia, a creekside park is losing ground to high tide, with erosion eating away six to eight feet of land. But local leaders are trying a new approach: instead of building hard walls, they're creating 'living shorelines' that mimic natural marshland. These living shorelines use plants and natural materials to stabilize the soil and absorb wave energy, giving the marsh room to migrate inland as sea levels rise. The project is a response to past failed attempts that relied on concrete and other hard structures. By working with nature rather than against it, the hope is to preserve Georgia's marshes for future generations. It's a smart, sustainable solution to a problem that's only going to get more pressing.
